speechtext:
Madam
Speaker, my major concern this afternoon is what I would almost consider sleazy behaviour on the part of some of our colleagues. There has been all sorts of manipulation. I was in the House this morning. I did not hear any suggestion of extending debate over the lunch hour and I have heard accusations flying back and forth.
The basis of this whole debate is to limit debate on a very important issue, the taking away from the people of Canada of their own airline and putting it into some so-called private sector that very likely could be controlled with all the manipulation by a foreign power. Because of that we need to have an extensive debate.
I become very concerned when I hear people talk about how we are holding up the business of the House. Granted, I have not been here for very long, but I do recognize the fact that this House has been sitting for over three years now. Come fall, it will be four years. All these Bills have now been listed. Did it take the Government until this last year to put these Bills on the legislative agenda? If that is the case, I hardly think it is fair to be accusing the other side of the House of holding things up.
I am also very concerned about the fact that this heavyhanded approach is being taken. There should be a broad discussion not just about what is happening to a major asset of Canada but about how the people of Canada feel about the implications of what could happen. Some of the statements made have been authoritarian and non-democratic. Certainly, a Government that is holding about 206 seats should not be backward about allowing us to put on record the feedback we are getting from our ridings.
I hear all this grandiose talk about extending debates, about the ability to extend debate but that no one is doing it. When I was not a Member of Parliament but an ordinary citizen, my understanding was that parliamentary reform was brought in so that there could be thoughtful consideration and serious debate on issues, so that there would be no night hearings and so that the regular timetable for the legislature could be followed so people could be responsible about their duties as Members of Parliament. Since I have been here, every now and then I hear that we need to have 15 people in the House or else they will extend the debate and shut off another Bill or we will be sitting all summer because the Government has not
Time Allocation
been able to get its legislative agenda together. That is certainly not the kind of Government Canadians thought they were getting when they saw that parliamentary reform was coming in. It really does make a farce of this structure that was supposed to make us responsible, make us thoughtful and help us bring issues forward, issues that we feel are important to our constituents and indeed important to the whole of Canada.
Certainly some of the words of the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart) which were quoted today were embarrassing. It certainly helped me to recognize what has been going on. Hon. Members are simply saying: "You did, you didn't, you did, you didn't," but are not really addressing the fact that we are supposed to be able to look at the whole issue of the privatization of Air Canada and its implications on isolated communities.
This country was brought together by transportation networks and systems. Yet this Government wants to use less than eight hours of debate and allow about 20 people to speak in the House and then say that is it, we know what is good for you and we will do it. Surely that is not the kind of democracy that we should have in the year 1988.
We do know that there has been more and more of a desire on the part of Canadians to know what is happening here. There have been many requests to ensure that we use technology so that people can know what is happening. Certainly, the televising of the House of Commons debates has given Canadians access to what is happening here, but on a day like today, I think what they are hearing and seeing is rather tragic.
This Government wants to railroad things through. There would be some excuse for it if it were a minority Government. As a minority Government, it would be a little more sensitive to procedure. If it were a minority Government, it would feel that it would have to do this and that in case the House falls. However, after having a great majority for three and a half years, the Government is now trying to rush everything through at the last minute and it is saying that it is the Opposition's fault because we will not allow debate. Where were the Bills? Just 10 days ago, we received a Bill that amends 27 statutes. It is absolutely ludicrous that the Government is doing that while saying that we are holding up debate. I think this is a real tragic day for democracy.
The Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) is very good at making a joke of everything. However, when he was in Opposition, he said some things with which we agree. He said, when he was on this side of the House, the following:
Where are all the defenders of the people on the other side of the House? They are going to come out of their trough in a few minutes. They will hear the bell and will have to break away from whatever trough they have their noses in at the moment. They will have to come into this House and says "Oink, oink". They will have to say "Aye, aye". They will have to say "Yes" to the stampeding of Parliament, to rushing this bill through the House. They will have to say "Yes" to the gutting of Parliament. They have to do the dirty work that the parliamentary assistants, assassins and eunuchs have asked them to do.

June 6, 1988
Time Allocation
The Hon. Member for St. John's West said that on June 9, 1981, when he was in opposition. In witnessing the kind of behaviour we have seen today, we have become witnesses to great hypocrisy. If there is cynicism on the part of the public, it is because members of the public know that politicians say one thing to them one day and do the opposite the next day.
Though I have not been a Member of the House for very long, I was certainly on the doorsteps of the people a year ago during the long by-election campaign. I had much opportunity to get a good sense of what the people of my constituency were saying and feeling. I got a feeling of a great sense of powerlessness from the people of my constituency. They felt that the Government would do whatever it liked, that it did not really care what was happening to any of us. We have witnessed that today.
We have heard the Government say that time allocation is not closure. For goodness sakes, who is it kidding, and what kind of procedures is it trying to play with? We know that the Government is limiting the time for debate on this particular Bill. I think that is unacceptable, particularly when it comes to such a serious Bill.
We know that the direction of air transportation policy will change, and it will be a major change. Some might think that that will be a benefit and others might think it will not be a benefit, but surely it is the role of the House of Commons to discuss that, have a full debate on it and have a vote on it.
The Government is terrified that there might be some actual facts that come out instead of a lot of gobbledegook. Government Members are terrified, so they want to stop the debate. They know that as soon as Canadians start to get a good sense of what is really happening in the country, they will not put their support behind the Government.
A few moments ago, government Members were saying that Canadians all supported free trade. They were talking to different Canadians than I have been talking to. Again, they do not want to talk about the substance of these Bills. As soon as we get into any substantive debate, we hear that we are trying to delay the business of the House of Commons.
I notice that my time is up. I think it really is a sad day for democracy when the Government is trying to push through a Bill like this and is terrified to let the facts come out.

subsubtopic: ALLOCATION OF TIME TO CONSIDER SECOND READING STAGE OF BILL C-129
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, much has been said with respect to the activities of this Government in attempting to stifle debate on this very important Bill. It is just ludicrous that the Government is attempting to choke off debate on this vitally important matter. Air Canada has been a Crown corporation for 51 years, yet the Government is apoplectic because we have debated this Bill for seven hours on second reading. It does not want to give the people of Canada the opportunity for the facts to come out. That is disgraceful. It is reprehensible. That is the kind of Government we have been getting for almost four years.
The Deputy Government House Leader said he had to put a limit on the debate because we would not sit extended hours on Friday. We were not prepared to oblige the Government in sitting well into the evening on Friday. He acted as though this was some kind of chastisement of the Opposition. This House adjourns on Friday afternoon for a very good reason. It allows Members of Parliament to get back to their constituencies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council

speechtext:
Now we hear from the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) whose constituents do not want him back in his constituency.
What happened is not only an abuse of the rights of Members of Parliament, but it is completely cutting the support out from underneath the Government's own proposition. It was that Government that brought forward the rule to adjourn on Friday afternoon at three o'clock. It was part of the Government's change to the rules of the House of Commons.
We have heard, of course, with great interest and amusement the comments made by the Hon. Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie) and the Hon. Member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart). I was just reading the Hon. Member's comments who said on February 12, 1981:
Is the reasoning behind closure that we have an 83-cent dollar-
As ludicrous as it was then, it is even more ludicrous today because the dollar is even lower than it was then.
This Bill is of vital importance to Canada. If it passes we will privatize one of the major Crown corporations, certainly one of the oldest. It has been in existence for 51 years. The Government, as we said, allowed Parliament to speak for only seven hours. Of course, the Conservatives are not willing to debate this. They just want to get it passed. They have presented only six speakers, less than either of the two opposition Parties, so they are not interested in presenting their side of the case because they really do not have much of a case to present. They want to make sure that the opposition Parties are unable to present their side of the House and we feel we do have a case.
Not only has the Government limited debate to approximately seven hours, this Bill was introduced for first reading on the Thursday before the long weekend in May. On Tuesday, when the House returned, the Government brought this Bill forward for second reading. It allowed one sitting day between first and second reading. The Government is adamant that the people of Canada not hear debate on this measure. It does not want the people to realize what this is going to do to transportation in Canada. It does not want the people to know what they are going to be losing through the giveaway of of this very valuable Crown corporation.
The Government does not want the people of this country to know that if it had done the same thing last summer when the market was higher, the country would have got millions of
June 6, 1988

dollars more for it. The Government is not only literally giving away this company to the private sector, but doing it at a time when the market is low.
The Government says it is not going to sell all of the shares of Air Canada, but it is not saying when it is going to sell any of the shares. It is going to sell some of the shares as soon as it possibly can. If it sells even one share of Air Canada, that Crown corporation stops being an arm of public policy to be used by Government or Parliament to the betterment and advantage of the people of Canada.
This is just a ludicrous situation. The Government said it had to give notice and limit the debate because, first, we would not sit extended hours on Friday. I have already mentioned that. Then it came through with this notice of motion on Friday, 15 minutes before we moved to deal with Private Members' Business. What the Government called consultation was to ask the opposition Parties how many speakers they proposed to put up. That is supposed to be consultation. There was no indication at all that it was going to limit debate.
The Government did this at a time when most Members were in their ridings, and no notice was given to either Members in the House or the various House Leaders. It waited until the last possible minute, knowing that as many Members as possible would be out of Ottawa. It is just incredible. Then the Government comes forward with the most ridiculous, most inane reasons for circumventing the rights of Parliament and the people of Canada. The new House rules may be an advantage but there are certain large gaps, and Standing Order 117 is one of them. In any event, the Government will not respect the spirit of the rules. It will use every little deficiency it sees in the rules to circumvent the rights of Parliament. That is a travesty and the Government is doing it more and more every day.
The Government expects goodwill from members of the Opposition. Certainly this opposition Party is prepared to give it if the Government has any sense of decency and any sense of acting in the best interests of Parliament and the people of this country. However, it has shown clearly it has not. Yet it will cry. It is the whiniest Government you will ever see. Any time members opposite feel someone steps on their toes, any time their noses are twigged, there is a wailing and hollering and beating of breasts and pounding of heads, a scene like you have never seen before. Yet we in the Opposition are supposed to be able to take that. We are supposed not only to have our rights trampled upon by the Government but we are supposed to allow the rights of the people of Canada to go undefended.
We are not going to do it. If we have to sit here all summer, every day, we are not going to do it. We are not going to do it because to do it would be a breakdown of the democracy which has existed in this country since it was founded.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will refrain from talking about parliamentary procedure because, like most Members here, I have not
Time Allocation
had the benefit of 15 or 20 years to learn all about it. To be quite honest with you, I do not believe that a lot of the people who have spoken today learned an awful lot in the time they have been here.
What I hear being debated now, does not make any sense. I thought everyone in the Opposition wanted to express their views about why Air Canada should not be privatized. Yet I have not heard anyone saying anything today about why Air Canada should not be privatized. They are talking about the rights of which they are being deprived by not being able to speak about it. Why do they not use the time they have today to talk about what a great disservice will be done to the people of Canada if we allow Air Canada to be privatized?
The reason I have not spoken on the Bill to date is because the people in my riding are saying that we should get it over with, that the mistake the Government is making is that it is not going all the way and allowing all the shares to be bought by the public.
I do not know what all the argument is about. I do know that if the motion before us is passed there will be another full day of debate. There have already been eight and a half hours of debate. Even then the debate will not be over.
I have heard Members talk about parliamentary reform. It certainly was not the Official Opposition that brought in parliamentary reform, it was the Progressive Conservative Government which brought in the parliamentary reform to which everyone is referring now. We saw the results of parliamentary reform last week when a private Member's Bill was passed in the House with Members on the government side voting in favour of Bill C-204. It does not seem that this Government wants to implement a dictatorship in the House of Commons. It is clear to me that the Government wants private Members to have a say in what is being passed in this House.
As I said, there would be another full day of debate and the Bill would then go to a legislative committee, which is another part of parliamentary reform brought in by the Government, where it would be debated by whichever Members are appointed to sit on the committee. The Bill would be debated in that committee for a number of days. I hear that some legislative committees have gone on for months, partly because the Opposition has used stalling tactics, similar to what they are doing today, so that the legislation would not come back to the House where it could be debated again at report stage.
After that, Madam Speaker, it will be debated again at third reading. When it leaves this Chamber and goes to the other Chamber, it will be debated once more.
Opposition Members obviously know that there are many Bills presently before the House and more Bills which will be brought in which contain good legislation for the country. They do not want them to come forward. They are hoping that after a while Members will get tired of the long hot summer

June 6, 1988
Time Allocation
and the legislation will be put on the back burner to be brought up later in the fall.
They talk about democracy. I was of the opinion that the people spoke in a democratic way when they elected the majority which the Government enjoys on this side of the Chamber. All the Members hear what their constituents tell them when they go home and they come here and act accordingly.
I think the Opposition is getting on with a lot of nonsense. What is the point of talking about what happened five years ago and ten years ago when Members who are no longer here argued back and forth about pieces of legislation? As far as I am concerned, we must now look to the present and the future, a future which is good for this country.
I believe that the privatization of Air Canada will be good for the country. That is what the people of Canada want. We should get the debate over with, get the legislation to committee, and let the people start buying shares in this government operated Crown corporation which they want to have privatized. I am sure that, the same as the other corporations which have been privatized, it will be good for the country.

speechtext:
Thank you, Madam Speaker. The guidelines of this new Government and this new Parliament were very simple and very straightforward and were very much appreciated by Canadians in general who gave the Government the majority it currently has as a result of a promise of national reconciliation through the introduction of consultation, co-operation, consensus and general civility. That has been disappearing very much over the last three and a half years. It has been disappearing, not only because of the actions of a few people in the opposition but because of the actions of the 206 Members who are now left on the government side.
We have seen a lack of consultation which has generated the particular brouhaha which we are into today. The Government House Leader and the House Leaders of the other two Parties failed to have meetings concerning the progress of the Air Canada Bill. Very few words even passed between them, let alone real consultation and valuable communication.
There has been a lack of co-operation because it is very difficult to co-operate if people do not communicate. Instead, we have degenerated to the point where the Government House Leader uses his substantial power in the House to move motions like those under Standing Order 117 to restrict debate on a particular piece of legislation. In this case, it is an Act to privatize Air Canada.
I suppose one can only expect that when there is a lack of consultation and co-operation, civility and consensus will soon disappear. We are now at the point where the House had almost fallen into total discord, as you pointed out and brought back to order again, Madam Speaker. The Mouse came back to order partly because many Members abandoned the House.
The Government is having great difficulty organizing its own business. There are some 41 uncompleted Bills that are on the Government's priority list of Bills which it would like to have debated and passed before the end of June, some 16 debating days from now. I do not believe that this House has ever generated that kind of productivity in passing legislation.
There were some productive days last week when I believe some four or five Bills dealing with Indian rights passed
June 6, 1988

through the House, some through all stages. That can happen when there is consensus and co-operation. However, that can only take place when it is accompanied by consultation.
Not only are there some 41 Bills on the priority list of the Government, there are another eight to ten Bills that it intends to introduce. Two Bills dealing with agriculture that were introduced today had been promised for some months. The legislation dealing with horse-racing had been discussed well before Christmas, and another Bill amending the Western Grain Stabilization Act was promised before Christmas. We are still waiting for amendments to the Canada Agricultural Products Standards Act which the Minister has been talking about since last summer. We have yet to see that Bill.
It is difficult to generate the kind of production the Government would like when it has not even completed the first stage of introducing and printing the Bill. Once Bills are before us, it is the right and duty of parliamentarians in opposition to look at them in a critical manner and see whether the proposed legislation is in the best interests of Canadians. If we have doubts or questions, it is our duty to present those arguments and those questions. That is why we are called the Loyal Opposition.
We began that process in the case of the Air Canada privatization Bill. We have been trying to find out why the Government wishes to begin the privatization process of a Crown corporation that has functioned efficiently and has served the country well for more than 50 years. That corporation has had profits exceeding its losses in the last 10 years amounting to $279.3 million.
Air Canada is not involved in a declining industry. The service provided by Air Canada is among the top 10 in the world according to all international objective observers. They recognize it as an efficient, well-managed and modern airline. It is recognized as among the most favoured airlines worldwide.
However, we are being told that this is not good enough and we must find another means of financing this corporation. We understand that it needs more equity to buy more equipment. There are a number of ways that this can be done, including the public issue of shares as decided upon by the Government. It could also be done through a commitment from the federal Treasury of another $200 million or $300 million and by expanding the equity shareholdings so that the corporation could borrow money that way. It is my understanding that even with the public issue of shares, the corporation's intention and requirement will be to go to the market to borrow money to make the necessary equipment purchases.
There is also the option of leasing equipment. We are not sure at this stage whether the Government and management of Air Canada fully investigated this alternative.
Apart from our concern about whether the Government has made the right choice in privatizing Air Canada, there are some aspects of the legislation that do not seem to make sense
Time Allocation
in terms of ownership and control. The Government is proposing to give control of 45 per cent of the shares to outside investors. We are told by Ministers involved with this legislation that the people who control the 45 per cent of the shares will have control of the corporation. That makes no sense to us. We believe it is undemocratic and not the proper way to give control.
At the same time, I believe the use of Standing Order 117 in this particular case is not the proper way for the Government to use its power. We believe that seven hours of debate on this very important matter is not enough. I urge the House to reject this motion to close the debate and to permit true democracy to continue functioning in a co-operative way which will provide a much better solution for the operation of the House and the country in general.
